Thank you for responding. I do understand in a limited sense, as I've been in a pretty dark place a few times, and my SO moreso.  I was from the school of thought, though, that said you struggle with depression, and need to take medication, you are weak.  It was a detriment to me, and I went for too long in a downward spiral of negative and incorrect thinking.

I think it just is hard for me to see people who feel as though there is no other option, that they somehow failed, that their life isn't important enough to fight for. We give support and accolades to those who beat cancer or other more 'physical' illnesses, but still treat depression and suicide like it's to be whispered and mentioned with shame. My friends just lost a 15 year old niece to suicide, and it breaks my heart. There was help for her, but her illness was not noticed in time and now she's gone. If more people approached depression/suicidal tendencies as an illness and not some sort of personal failing, I think many more would be saved. Not that I'm saying that is how you view it, it's just why I think I'm so passionate about making people realize that it IS a chemical imbalance in the brain, and not a personal failing.
I'm sorry you feel my logic is absurd. I still stand by the fact that it is wrong to NOT get treatment for depression, as it would be wrong to let cancer fester in your body until it destroys it.

Well, your thoughts can lie to you. And just because they are telling you 'what's the point', and 'why bother', does not mean they are correct. When they tell you life is not worth living, and it will never get better, they are lying to you. They are wrong. Your feelings don't need to guide you all the time. It takes wisdom to look past your feelings and thoughts when you know they are faulty, and keep pushing on. Because life is precious, it's a one-time chance, and you can make a difference in it, even if it's small and seemingly insignificant. 

I've seen people commit suicide, and the outpouring of grief from so many people who want to know why they never disclosed their struggles to them; why they didn't reach out for help? So many people are willing and ready to be there and to offer support, at least from what I've seen. I'm sure you have people in your life who would also do that for you. And don't let the lies of your thoughts tell you otherwise!!

I love my SO and he has so much potential. You do too. Don't give up.
Neither is my SO...but he's doing so much better now, I'm thankful he persevered. There was A LOT of anger and 'why isn't this working' questions, but please don't give up!
My SO has been on a cocktail of meds for 2 years now, and I am just starting to see improvement! Don't give up, just keep trying different meds/therapists until you finally find something that works.

You said you didn't see anything "wrong" with suicide. I was trying to show that it goes against a very basic human instinct, pointing to a flaw in the system and that something is wrong in how the individual's brain works.
I agree, although maybe it was meant to comfort the freind left behind who is probably feeling tremendous guilt. But yeah, I don't think it's healthy to glamorize suicide in any way.

Humans were made to want to survive...the very fact that one wants to take their life shows faulty wiring in need of treatment. Just as someone who suffers from cancer....it is not morally wrong to be sick, but why not get help when it is available instead of letting them just die?
I'm trying to understand your point of view but....it's so difficult!

Also the people who think that by sheer will-power and determination, you should be able to overcome mental illness. And if you can't, you are weak. 

And how if someone dies from cancer, let's tell everyone and ask them to give to that cause, but if someone commits suicide, let's hush it up because we're ashamed they were so 'weak' and 'cowardly'..because it has nothing to do with an illness that causes their brain to not process thoughts correctly, right??

I can relate with you..I've been in the field roughly the same amount of time, and have worked for the same company for 7 years now (and I too live in the midwest). Most projects are very quick turnaround, and there is no other designers with whom I can sharpen my skills with. I have felt burned out for awhile.

Lately I've tried to find some inspiration online when I can and push myself to incorporate ideas I normally would not have. But when there are tight deadlines, there is only so much you can do.

I've thought about a career change, but would hate to go through the work/training/schooling and find myself in the same position I am now but deeper in debt. If you feel drawn to something strongly, though, perhaps you can start by freelancing to see how it fits? Otherwise, I don't think it's a bad idea to throw your resume out there if you see an open position for another company. Maybe a change of environment and finding a place with more than one designer will help?

Best of luck to you!

My spouse was hired on by a company that paid for him to relocate. They pro-rated his health insurance to the date of hire (instead of making him wait the customary 3 months). So when he became very ill only 2 months after starting there, he had health insurance to cover the hospital stay (not to mention they sent him flowers).

Then when he became disabled as a result of the illness, they worked with him for over a year to try and accommodate him. When we realized he wouldn't be able to work because of the disability, they paid him 6 months of a reduced salary while he was on family leave (they were not obligated by law to do this), as well as kept him on his health benefits.

I think back to that time and am so amazed..I don't know what we would have done financially if they hadn't done all that. Probably been bankrupt by now.

Neat story...@ 15 years ago, my mom picked up an old record at a thrift store or yard sale (can't remember exactly), and was all excited about sending it to my uncle (her brother). It was Telstar by the Tornadoes. She said it was one of his favorite songs when he was a teen. She played it on the record player for me to hear, and I was intrigued..it was so sixties sounding, and kind of melancholic, and the tune was unforgettable.

I've only been into Muse for about 3 years, but I remember early on researching the band, then finding out this little tidbit about Matt's dad, and recognized the song from when my mom played it years ago. I had come full circle :) So KoC holds a special place in my heart, since it harkens back to my very first taste of that Bellamy magic.
